facts.statement: Ngwevu is a massospondylid sauropodomorph dinosaur that lived in the Lower Jurassic of South Africa.
facts.quote: Ngwevu is a genus of massospondylid sauropodomorph dinosaur from the Lower Jurassic of South Africa.

facts.statement: The only known specimen of Ngwevu was discovered in 1978 by James William Kitching on Tevrede Farm in the Fouriesburg district of South Africa.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen was discovered in 1978 by James William Kitching in the Tevrede Farm, located in Fouriesburg district, South Africa.

facts.statement: Ngwevu was originally thought to be a specimen of Massospondylus but was reclassified as a new genus and species in 2019.
facts.quote: The specimen was initially considered a specimen of the genus Massospondylus but in 2019 was designated as a new genus and species Ngwevu ntloko

facts.statement: The genus Ngwevu is known from a single fossil specimen, cataloged as BP/1/4779.
facts.quote: The genus Ngwevu is known from only one specimen, BP/1/4779

facts.statement: Ngwevu is distinguished from other sauropodomorphs by a unique set of 16 traits, including a ridge on the backside of the jugal bone.
facts.quote: Ngwevu can be distinguished from other sauropodomorphs based on a unique combination of 16 traits, including one unique feature: a ridge on the lateral surface of the backside of the jugal.

facts.statement: Histological studies indicate the Ngwevu holotype was an adult approximately 10 years old when it fossilized, ruling out the hypothesis that it was a juvenile.
facts.quote: However, histological study of the holotype of Ngwevu suggests it was an adult (about 10 years old) when it fossilized, rejecting this hypothesis as well.

facts.statement: The wider snout of Ngwevu suggests it had a more generalist diet compared to the more selective Massospondylus carninatus.
facts.quote: The snout of Ngwevu is wider than that of Massospondylus carninatus, and the describing authors propose that it signifies a more generalist rather than selective diet.

facts.statement: Ngwevu likely had a stronger bite than Massospondylus carinatus due to its robust jaw and skull features, suggesting they occupied different ecological niches.
facts.quote: The holotype's robust jaw and skull features, including a broad palate and short snout, may have given it a stronger bite than M. carinatus, suggesting niche partitioning between these two species.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis places Ngwevu intloko within the family Massospondylidae.
facts.quote: A phylogenetic analysis conducted in the describing paper corroborates this, placing Ngwevu intloko in the Massospondylidae.

facts.statement: Ngwevu fossils are found in the Clarens Formation, dating to the Pliensbachian to early Toarcian stages.
facts.quote: The strata which preserved the specimen was located in the Clarens Formation, which is Pliensbachian-early Toarcian in age.

facts.statement: Ngwevu lived between 201.4 and 192.9 million years ago, spanning the Hettangian to Sinemurian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Hettangian to Sinemurian (201.4 to 192.9 million years ago)

facts.statement: Some paleontologists hypothesized that Ngwevu might be a younger, less developed specimen of Massospondylus, though this was later rejected.
facts.quote: Another hypothesis presumed the differences found in Ngwevu could be attributed to a less advanced ontogenetic stage, with some paleontologists considering it to be a younger specimen of Massospondylus.

rejected.statement: Researchers note that Ngwevu was proportionately more robust than specimens of the related genus Massospondylus.
rejected.quote: The describing authors of Ngwevu also noted that Ngwevu was proportionately more robust than specimens of Massospondylus.
